texto_fonte:
The shape of water at a key tau hotspot helps drive dementia-linked clumping
Diseases such as Alzheimer's and frontotemporal dementia are considered neurodegenerative tauopathies, in which tau proteins in the brain misfold and lead to cognitive decline. Until now, it has been unclear how misfolded tau recruits other seemingly healthy tau and causes it to misfold and clump.
A new study led by Northwestern University researchers, in collaboration with researchers at the University of California, Santa Barbara, found that tau vulnerable to misfolding carries a single dominant hotspot. That site binds to the matching site on a neighboring tau or on a tau at the end of an existing fibril, and the incoming tau then misfolds to match.
The hotspot is hydrated by water that wraps over and protects a hydrophobic site, and releasing that water pulls the two together.
This finding could help scientists diagnose tauopathies, block misfolded tau from converting other normal tau to misfolded shapes and design therapeutic solutions in the future.
The study was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
"Once you know that aggregation-prone tau proteins always have a hotspot that is first attracted to the same site of tau that is stacked to fibrils, then you know there's always some part of the protein that you can target to neutralize," said Songi Han, senior author of the study. "If you know where to block its action of misfolding, you could block it to prevent it from propagating."
Han is a Mark and Nancy Ratner professor of chemistry at Northwestern's Weinberg College of Arts and Sciences and the vice chair of the American Chemical Society's physical chemistry division.
The puzzle of tau's precise alignment
When it comes to understanding why they misfold and propagate their misfolded shape, tau proteins have been a black box for researchers. Unlike other proteins, tau protein monomers are not structured. They stack together, however, in perfect register to form long fibrils, with every tau molecule adopting the same shape upon attaching to the growing fibril end.
How do thousands of noodle-like, unstructured molecules know to find each other, recreate that same misfolded shape and stack in perfect alignment, like a tower of poker chips thousands high? This is where Han and her team stepped in.
"The proteins have to misfold and neatly stack to fibrils to elongate while propagating the same misfolded shape, and the only way that this process is forever is if the same site of the protein stacks to the same," Han said. "If you have a tiny mismatch in the alignment of the tau shapes that stack to the fibril end, the structure will eventually stop growing."
The chemistry of tau proteins dictates the architecture of the fibrils they build, with each misfolded tau stacking on top of the one beneath it to hold the fibril together. These tau fibrils build up inside neurons as neurofibrillary tangles and disrupt communication among neurons. When the cell dies and the misfolded tau proteins are released, they can "infect" other tau proteins that are floating around and waiting to be used.
Water caps bring hotspots together
Like all proteins in a cell, tau is surrounded by water. But that water does not interact with every part of the protein in the same way. Some regions readily attract and interact with water. But other regions are hydrophobic, meaning they tend to repel water.
Han and her team found unusual water structuring around hotspots within tau's hydrophobic regions. At these spots, water forms a cap reminiscent of ice, except that the water molecules stay dynamic. These caps mark where the two tau molecules will meet.
"You have a certain site, and water cannot quite coat it because it doesn't like water. But that part still needs to be protected, because if you don't, then the protein crashes out and is no longer available," Han said. "What water tends to do is build a stabilizing cap around it, and basically these water caps attract each other."
When two hotspots meet, the capping water is released, and the energy gained by freeing it locks them together. This ensures the tau proteins will line up the same way every time. When the team capped the hotspot with a chemical tag, the fibrils stopped growing. Capping two other sites away from the hotspot did not stop fibril growth.
Targeting hotspots and building disease models
Now that researchers understand how tau continues to cause new tau to misfold and where this interaction begins, scientists can focus their efforts on blocking that hotspot before the fibrils recruit more tau and spread to other neurons.
"We might have found a shortcut for the pharmacist or biochemist because instead of searching for everything, we can say, 'Look for that hotspot. That's the spot that matters,'" Han said. "We are trying to give it the principle of how it works so that others can find solutions better, faster or more rationally."
Understanding how tau works also could allow researchers to create synthetic tau fibrils that mimic the various tauopathy diseases and to develop diagnostic and therapeutic agents. Researchers currently do not have good models for neurodegenerative disease research.
"In order to cure a disease, one needs to be able to recreate it," Han said. "There's a real problem that disease-mimicking tau fibrils cannot be synthetically made easily. It's really difficult to try to do any development with human patient tissue."
To synthetically make a protein, researchers need to understand how the protein works. This study could be a critical step in creating synthetic proteins, and not necessarily just tau proteins, for future medical research.
Publication details
A water-pinning hot spot drives templated tau aggregation, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (2026). DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2611158123
Journal information: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

texto_fonte:
AI platform and database map protein phase separation across species
Scientists at Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU Singapore) have developed an AI-powered database and a platform that could enable researchers to more accurately predict which proteins undergo phase separation—a process through which proteins in cells separate like oil droplets in water.
The tools are the result of a systematic analysis of predicted phase-separating proteins from various living things, including animals, plants, fungi and single-celled organisms such as bacteria. From their analyses, the scientists also uncovered fundamental insights about the phase separation process.
The research was led by Professor Miao Yansong from the School of Biological Sciences and the Institute for Digital Molecular Analytics and Science (IDMxS) at NTU, in collaboration with Professor Gao Weibo from NTU's School of Electrical and Electronic Engineering. It could be applied to advance the understanding of diseases and aging, as well as to improve crops.
Both AI tools and the research findings have been reported in the journal Molecular Plant.
Predicting which proteins separate
Phase-separating proteins separate from their surroundings and concentrate into droplet-like compartments, enabling cells to bring molecules together and accelerate or suppress reactions to respond rapidly to stress.
When phase separation is altered, these proteins can form abnormal condensates or aggregates, which are associated with diseases, including cancer and neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's disease. In plants, changes in phase separation are linked to impaired stress responses and lowered immunity against microbial pathogens.
Identifying proteins that undergo phase separation and determining how this behavior is regulated are important for applications ranging from biomedical research on diseases and aging to devising approaches for sustainable agriculture.
However, accurate prediction remains challenging because phase-separating proteins assemble dynamically into complex structures and interact with numerous cellular components. Addressing these challenges requires comprehensive experimental data sets and systems-level information across diverse organisms.
In addition, most collections focus predominantly on full-length proteins while underrepresenting validated negative experimental results, truncated proteins and sequence variants like mutations. This imbalance often causes predictive models to overestimate a protein's tendency to condense.
To address this gap, the NTU team used large language AI models to systematically mine scientific papers indexed in PubMed. The researchers extracted information about experimentally tested proteins and their phase behavior before manually reviewing the results to ensure scientific accuracy.
The resulting database, PLATO, contains 5,118 unique protein sequences, including more than 3,600 proteins that undergo phase separation and 1,300 that do not. It captures shortened versions of proteins, mutations and engineered variants that are rare in existing phase-separation data sets. This makes PLATO a valuable resource for developing more accurate AI tools that predict phase-separating proteins.
Predicting protein partners
Many different molecules, such as nucleic acids, also interact with phase-separating proteins to organize them into droplets.
To investigate these interactions, the scientists also created PhaseHub. They first used MolPhase, a machine-learning algorithm that they previously developed, to predict phase-separating proteins from 1,106 species. They then combined MolPhase results with experimental data on protein abundance and interactions to identify these multicomponent compartments in various biological processes.
This approach allows researchers to search for a protein or submit a sequence, examine its predicted phase-separation properties, visualize potential interactions and explore features that influence molecular interactions, such as continuous stretches of repeated amino acids known as homorepeats.
The scientists found that eukaryotes—organisms whose cells contain a nucleus—generally have a substantially higher proportion of proteins that may undergo phase separation than organisms like bacteria that do not have a nucleus. Among organisms with smaller genomes, the proportion of phase-separating proteins increased with genome size before reaching a plateau.
The findings suggest a balance between genomic DNA content and phase-separation capacity. Larger genomes code for more phase-separating proteins, which could enhance cellular processes. However, an excessive tendency to condense may increase the risk of harmful aggregation.
"Our work provides a comprehensive framework for understanding phase-separating proteins, which will serve as a valuable resource for researchers in the field," said Dr. Liang Qiyu, a research fellow at IDMxS, who was the first author of both papers.
"By leveraging AI and systems biology to integrate experimental data with findings from existing literature, our platforms offer accurate, user-friendly tools for predicting and identifying proteins that may undergo phase separation. These tools will advance investigations into the roles of these proteins in agriculture as well as human diseases," said Miao.
Publication details
Qiyu Liang et al., PLATO: A new benchmark for phase separation prediction, Molecular Plant (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.molp.2026.07.015
Qiyu Liang et al., From pan-life phase insights to PhaseHub: Analyzing protein condensate complexity, Molecular Plant (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.molp.2026.07.019

candidato.titulo: Closing the reality gap: Why real-time execution has become the new competitive advantage
candidato.resumo: Daifuku's Cecile Dick-Calmes said success is no longer measured solely by automation density or equipment utilization. The post Closing the reality gap: Why real-time execution has become the new competitive advantage appeared first on The Robot Report .

texto_fonte:
Organizations across the supply chain continue to invest heavily in automation. Yet for many warehouse and distribution leaders, the expected gains in productivity, throughput, and agility remain elusive.
The issue is rarely a lack of technology. More often, it is a lack of synchronization.
As fulfillment networks become increasingly complex, a new challenge has emerged: the growing gap between what digital systems believe is happening and what is actually occurring on the warehouse floor. This disconnect, which can be described as the “reality gap,” is becoming one of the most significant barriers to operational performance.
Closing that gap is quickly becoming a defining capability for high-performing operations.
The new operational challenge: When digital and physical reality diverge
Modern warehouses generate enormous volumes of data. Inventory transactions, equipment status updates, labor activities, transportation events, and order flows are all captured and processed by various systems.
Yet data alone does not guarantee operational awareness.
In many facilities, information arrives too late, remains trapped in silos, or lacks the context needed to support timely decisions. As a result, operational leaders are often responding to events that have already occurred rather than actively managing conditions as they unfold.
The consequences are familiar:
- Inventory records that do not accurately reflect physical reality
- Congestion that develops before being detected
- Bottlenecks that spread through interconnected processes
- Labor and equipment deployed based on outdated conditions
- Delays that compound across the fulfillment network
The reality gap is not simply a technology problem. It is an execution problem.
Why automation alone is no longer enough
For decades, the primary objective of warehouse automation was straightforward: reduce manual handling and improve efficiency within individual processes.
That approach delivered significant gains.
Today, however, automation environments are substantially more sophisticated. Facilities often operate multiple automated subsystems simultaneously, each capable of performing its intended function effectively. The challenge is ensuring those systems collectively support broader operational objectives.
A warehouse may have advanced automation, sophisticated software, and highly optimized processes. Yet if these elements are not continuously aligned around current operating conditions, inefficiencies remain.
This is why leading organizations are shifting their focus from automation itself to orchestration.
Automation enables movement. Orchestration enables performance. The distinction is becoming increasingly important as supply chains face greater volatility, labor constraints, and demands for faster fulfillment.
The rise of real-time execution
Closing the reality gap requires organizations to move beyond periodic visibility and toward real-time execution. Real-time execution is the ability to continuously sense operational conditions, evaluate changing circumstances, and coordinate responses across people, processes, and technology.
Rather than relying on static plans, organizations can dynamically adapt to what is actually occurring in the facility at any given moment.
This capability rests on several foundational principles:
- Continuous awareness of operational conditions
- Immediate detection of exceptions and disruptions
- Dynamic allocation of work and resources
- Rapid adaptation to changing demand and workloads
- Coordinated decision-making across interconnected systems
The objective is not simply faster data collection. The objective is faster, better decisions. In increasingly complex fulfillment environments, decision speed is becoming as important as processing speed.
From connected operations to intelligent operations
Many organizations have spent the past decade focused on connectivity, integrating systems, collecting data, and creating visibility.
The next stage of operational maturity is intelligence.
The most effective operations are not necessarily those with the largest volume of data. They are the ones that can translate operational signals into action before small issues become significant disruptions.
This shift is changing how leaders think about operational performance.
Success is no longer measured solely by automation density or equipment utilization. Increasingly, it is measured by how effectively an organization can detect change, make decisions, and execute those decisions in real time. In other words, competitive advantage is migrating from assets to agility.
The strategic benefits of closing the reality gap
Organizations that successfully close the reality gap typically see benefits that extend well beyond efficiency gains.
They become more resilient when disruptions occur. They improve consistency and service quality because decisions are based on current conditions rather than historical assumptions. They create better utilization of resources by balancing workloads more effectively. They reduce operational friction that often leads to excessive labor demands, equipment bottlenecks, and inventory discrepancies.
Most importantly, they build operations capable of adapting continuously rather than reacting after the fact.
In an environment where customer expectations, labor availability, and market conditions are constantly changing, adaptability has become one of the most valuable operational capabilities an organization can develop.
Looking ahead
The future of warehouse performance will not be defined solely by the adoption of automation technologies. It will be defined by how effectively organizations connect planning with execution and digital intelligence with physical operations.
As facilities become more automated and supply chains grow more complex, the ability to maintain alignment between operational reality and system awareness will become increasingly critical.
The question for supply chain leaders is no longer whether automation is necessary. Now, the question is whether their organization can turn automation into coordinated, real-time execution.
Because in modern fulfillment operations, the greatest inefficiencies often exist not in the movement of products, but in the gap between knowing what is happening and acting on it.
Cecile Dick-Calmes is a content marketing strategist and creative leader with experience in B2B and B2C digital marketing. She is currently the inbound marketing manager at Daifuku Wynright and previously worked at The Boeing Co. as a community manager and at Hainan Airlines as the digital marketing lead.

candidato.titulo: Presentation: You Can't Trust Your AI Bill. And Neither Can I
candidato.resumo: Erik Peterson discusses why AI spend is eclipsing cloud bills, triggering a major software engineering cost crisis. He explains tokenmaxxing, unit economics, forced developer promotions, and why fully autonomous AI will write, deploy, and govern code by 2028. By Erik Peterson

texto_fonte:
Transcript
Erik Peterson: I'm going to talk a little bit about the bill. There was a lot of conversation about all the great things that we're building. I think we really have gotten to a place where we're building an enormous amount of great things, but the bill comes due at some point. I wanted to share some of the things that I've been seeing, my company's been seeing, and make some wild-ass guesses about where I think it's all going. You all can hold me accountable to that. I can tell you, quite frankly, that it's a mess. Who am I? I'm Erik Peterson. I'm the CTO and founder of the company CloudZero. I started the company here in Boston in 2016. Coming up in August, almost on 10 years. It's been a wild and crazy ride over the last 10 years. Nobody could have predicted what's going on right now, or maybe somebody did. I'm sure somebody did. CloudZero is the financial control plane for cloud and AI. I'll share some of the data. Six months ago, we noticed something interesting happening in the bill.
Rise of AI
We are here. Really, we are here. This is what is happening. It is an amazing time that we can live in that if I want a money-flaming meteor and pounding it into the earth, I can just have whatever I want to create in front of me. How much did that cost to generate? I'm going to say this a few times today. I used to say every engineering decision is a buying decision. We are now in a world where every decision is a buying decision. I need to do some research, I'm going to go to Perplexity. I'm going to write some code, I'm going to go to Claude. I'm going to build some images, maybe I'll go to ChatGPT. Before I send that email, before I finish that thought, I am putting that information probably through some LLM somewhere. That costs money. Somehow, we've gotten ourselves in a situation where every thought we have is now monetized.
It sounds a little dystopian. Maybe it's the evolution of the human race. I certainly hope so. We are here. It costs money. The bill comes due. The bill is a little crazy. We have amazing statements like this being made. How many people saw this? Think about that. Take whatever your salary is, and if you don't spend half of that salary by the end of the year, Jensen doesn't think you're a great engineer. He's going to lose his mind. I think this may have kicked off, or maybe it was right in the heart of the tokenmaxxing universe. Tokenmaxxing, what is that rot upon the world? This is single-handedly probably the most expensive vanity metric in the history of IT. It's really hard to estimate exactly what that is. It's somewhere on the order of $5 billion to $15 billion. How many people had a boss or a manager or a CEO who was looking at the AI leaderboard — they're calling it a leaderboard — to figure out who in their organization was doing what they hoped they were doing with AI.
Did they know? No. They knew for a fact that if you weren't spending money, something must have been wrong. This is the craziest thing ever. Here we are. This term, I think, was invented back in March. It was declared over in May. I think it's still going. I think we're still living this. What has happened over the past couple months is pretty indicative of what's to come.
I think AI is coming for your jobs, too. If that meteor wasn't scary enough. Last year, I would say this definitively is not true. I was wrong. Last year, I would have said, you're not going to lose your job to AI. You're going to lose your job to somebody using AI. I actually think what's happening is we are getting a promotion. It's a forced promotion. We're going to have to accept it and change. Nothing drives this point home for me more than actually a story from my past. One of my first jobs in IT where I was working at a computer support job and had a couple of nice ladies walk into my office. They said, we used to work in this office and then you people with your computers showed up. We were six of us on typewriters. Typewriters had a real feel to them, a computer, soulless.
You guys took our jobs. Typewriter has shown up in the AI era. We've got to go figure out what promotion we're going to get. I think next year we're going to be really wondering, what is our job now? It's definitely not going to be about doing the work. It's going to be probably about managing the work. Our taste might be the only thing that matters.
The Promise versus Reality
This is going to color the whole conversation we're going to have today. This is the promise versus reality. Don't worry, AI is not coming for your job. I think it's coming for your job. Don't worry, tokens are going to get cheaper. Actually, tokens have gotten cheaper but we're spending a little bit more. In fact, they've gotten a lot cheaper. AI makes us all more productive. How many people here feel more productive? I feel pretty productive. If I look at the number of lines of code, the number of PRs, the number of commits, it all is up and to the right. Some days I wonder, am I churning? We're still bad at measuring developer productivity. We haven't really quite figured this out. I think it's going to only get worse. Don't worry, the cost curve only goes down. Actually, our spend is pretty much tripled and only going up.
Storyline
Here's the storyline for today: confession, the eclipse, the inversion, the aftermath, and then hopefully some things that we can take with us after this that will help us.
Act 1: The Confession - You Can't Trust Your AI Bill, Neither Can I
I got a confession to make. I built a company that built the category, and I can't actually fully trust our bill either. I spend all day long looking at the data that comes from the cloud providers, the AI providers, random people on the street sending cost data into our system. It is a mess. Anybody who tells you that this stuff is clean and easy and it's just data is forgetting something. We all know that just data is there be dragons there. When we look deeper into the AI bill, actually, like what's behind that? Is it just inference? Is it just tokens in and tokens out? There's a lot going on inside of there. A lot of it is buried and hidden and not even ever revealed to us. It's just charged to us. At least we have the benefit when we look at the Amazon or the Google bill to see that I spent this much on EC2 and this much on S3 and this much on who knows what.
At least I have an itemized list. We have somehow reverted to the world where right now I get a bill that is the equivalent of what I've been getting from my power company for the last 100 years. You spent $500 on 10,000 kilowatt hours. Doing what? Getting what? Providing what? Did I leave the lights on? Was the oven on? AC? I don't know. Somehow, we're back to where we were 100 years ago that hasn't changed, 10,000 kilowatts, a million tokens. There's a lot to try to unpack behind the invisible, so much so, actually, that folks at the University of Maryland had to go come up with an entirely new approach to get at it. They call it CoIn, the cost of the invisible. They found that there's just a ridiculous amount of invisible spend happening behind the scenes. What you get shown on the screen isn't necessarily what you're paying for. Sometimes it's built around changes in the model, changes in the weather, changes in things that aren't revealed to us. It's 10,000 kilowatt hours. Is it because a tree branch hit the power line and suddenly the power got a little weirder? We don't know. It's actually gotten a lot worse.
Nobody agrees on the unit. If we try to look at the data that's actually coming in, nobody can agree on exactly what it is or what it means. We've got different formulas for code, for images, for audio. Some of this stuff charges us for silence. Some of this stuff charges us differently. It's all a mess. They use different terms, different formats, different schemas, different everything. It causes huge problems when you try to bring it all together. They're all random vendor implementation details. We've rolled back 100 years. The prices themselves also don't make any sense. I really want to know why o1 still exists. It's 7.5 times more expensive. There's zero reason for you to use it. There's vastly superior models for vastly less cost but it's still there. Somebody, some enterprise somewhere has an agent running in a basement that is consuming tokens that's probably keeping OpenAI afloat.
They thank you for your service. Other providers, I think Google turns off models after a year. Maybe they're doing everyone a favor. OpenAI is leaving stuff around for a really long time. Or maybe that was Microsoft. Pick a region. You'd think, I'll just keep it in the U.S. That'll be cheaper. Instead of multi-region. Multi-region sounds expensive. No, pick a region that's more expensive. Don't pick a region, you're going to spend more. That's a feature. They change how they tokenize things. Token costs go up 35%. All this stuff changes and none of it is really under your control, except maybe the model you pick. The APIs themselves, the ones where we get this data, they're broken. We don't need to tell a story about uptime and availability these days, which is fascinating how unimportant that number seems to have become if you've been a GitHub customer for a while.
It's happening everywhere. It's like the old days, "AWS is down. Let's all go out for a bite to eat." "Claude's down today. I'm not going to get any work done." When we're trying to get the cost data, daily 500s. When we're trying to get information from OpenAI, daily 500s. Cursor, one bad record in there, the whole thing just blows up. It is a mess. This is just what happened in the last 90 days. If you think that this is happening over some long period of evolution, no, it's not. It's happening in real time. This presentation actually was the hardest presentation I think I've ever had to create, because I'd write something down. Then I'd look at the information the next day, and I realized, new stuff out. It's wrong already. We didn't even have a proper API to pull Anthropic Enterprise billing data down, until March. If you're on claude.com, you could get your billing data. If you're on claude.ai, two vastly different platforms, you could not. Except screenshot it, and download a spreadsheet from their website. All of this churn, just in the last 90 days.
Act 2: The Eclipse - All Cost is Eclipsing the Cloud Bill
What is happening? It's pretty simple. AI is going to eclipse the cloud bill. Cloud and all its growth, all its craziness, all the billions trending towards trillions, if we look at just what's happened in the last couple months, that was the warm-up match to what's coming. Anthropic's like up and to the right is truly insane. Nothing like this has ever occurred before. This is the warm-up match. I believe all cloud spend is going to be absorbed by AI. There's only going to be one thing, it's going to be AI. Just days ago, all these crazy things happened. We're talking billions if not trillions of dollars here exchanging hands. Flowing, who knows where it's going? People making huge claims about how compute is going to be spent. It is an entirely different ball game. We thought cloud was expensive. No. That is a rounding error to what is getting spent right now.
I think that is going to lead to a disruption timeline that is moving faster than any of us here are prepared for. I thought I was crazy. Actually, a lot of people thought I was crazy. I started committing myself to only using AI to create code in January of 2025. By the middle of the year, I was convinced that all code is going to be written by AI. If you talk to anybody in California, they were convinced too. Everybody outside was like, I don't know. How many people think that all code in the future is not going to be written by AI? We'll come talk about that in a year. It's all going to get written by AI. I think it's going to happen faster than anyone thinks. I think that what we'll end up with is something I call the fully autonomous cloud, which is AI writing the code, AI deploying the code, AI managing the code.
It all is running in an autonomous fashion. The cloud as we know it is going away. It is going to disappear. My bet is that it's all done and figured out by 2028. We'll see. You can take the safe bet, but I don't think I've been aggressive enough. It won't be the financing mechanism. Interesting point of fact is that every AI startup combined is still eight times short of the total AI CapEx spend of all the cloud providers. There's still this huge gap. Where's that gap getting made up? I mean $80 billion here. It just seems like $80 billion is such a small number. What is going on? They're both burning cash if we look at both of the giants out there. They think about their numbers drastically different. Anthropic says that they're profitable 5% return based on how they built their numbers and built their books.
OpenAI has got a negative 122%. Crazy. They're both looking at about 80% margins on their API calls. They are making money. This AI cost crisis feeds the narrative as well. This is probably the most profitable supply chain in tech ever. These are real numbers. What you get charged and what we're paying. We're so driven to grab this right now that we stop paying attention at some point. We've seen the circle chart a few times. The circle is real. Every time I turn around there's a new box to add to it that's feeding the circle. I think as long as it just keeps flowing and spinning, we're going to be ok. Just keep spinning. Just keep spinning, we'll be ok. I hope. Otherwise, it's sticks and rocks and stones.
Act 3: The Inversion - The Cost to BUILD is Eclipsing the Cost to SERVE
The inversion is this magical thing that some CFOs have started to notice which is the cost to build is now the most expensive thing, not the cost to serve. Cost to serve was what I was spending to deliver cloud computing and deliver services to my customers. The cost to build is what we're spending to build this thing, to maintain this thing, to deploy this thing. Somehow the cost to build became more expensive. I know a lot of you have probably heard of Jevons Paradox. I don't think a lot of people actually stop and talk about just how freaking old this thing is, 1865. I love it. We're talking about a power bill that looks like what Westinghouse would have given me 200 years ago. We're talking about Stanley Jevons worrying about coal. Just really internalize this, because Jevons Paradox is at the crux of it all.
The more efficient we make a thing the more we consume of that thing. We're making it very efficient, or at least attempting to. This is what it looks like in reality. candidato.titulo: AMD debuts Helion reference design for agentic AI servers with up to 32,768 Zen 6 ‘Venice’ cores
candidato.resumo: At the OCP Global Summit, AMD revealed Helion, a rack-scale reference design for agentic AI that can house up to 32,768 Zen 6 CPU cores.

texto_fonte:
Updated 10/12/26 at 12:01pm ET: AMD originally said the Helion rack would ship in the first half of 2027, but it has revised the release date to November 2026. We've updated the headline and featured image. We also corrected an error where OpenU trays were marked as 21mm wide instead of 21 inches wide.
AMD is bringing a new reference rack-scale design to the data center ecosystem with Helion. It’s a standardized, 21-inch rack reference design that will complement the Helios rack AMD revealed at OCP Global Summit last year. This year, we have Helion, which AMD says can house up to 32,768 Zen 6 cores in a CPU-only deployment using the dense 256-core design available with the EPYC ‘Venice’ 9996.
The rack design is standardized, based on the Open Compute Project’s ORv4 specification, which is slightly wider and taller than a standard IT rack. Helion is designed to support 44 OpenU trays, which are 21 inches wide and 48mm tall, slightly larger than a standard EA1-310 tray. AMD says the reference design supports both air-cooled and direct liquid-cooled deployments.
The design is also compliant with OCP’s DC-MHS (Data Center Modular Hardware System) standard. MHS is designed to bring “interoperability between key elements of data center, edge, and enterprise infrastructure,” according to OCP.
Although AMD has renders of the design you can see in the presentation below, it won’t actually sell racks. This is a reference design that AMD is contributing to OCP, and OEMs and ODMs will actually bring that design to market. AMD didn’t share partners supporting Helion during a pre-briefing with the press. The company says CEO Lisa Su will announce partners during the lead keynote at the OCP Global Summit later today.
AMD also didn’t share deployment partners, though it suggested that Helios customers will also deploy Helion racks.
Unlike Helios, which is built for AI training and inference, Helion is a more flexible rack solution primarily focused on CPUs. In a CPU-only deployment, the design can hold up to 128 EPYC 9996 CPUs, bringing that impressive 32,768 core count per rack. This configuration would likely look something like an agentic AI sandbox system, which is then connected to an inference system.
This model for personal AI agents is in use today, both in Meta’s Muse and OpenAI Dots. Each user has a sandbox with a slice of compute from the host system, with the backbone of an inference server. Some workloads are handled on those CPU-only servers, such as building software, but the heavy-duty AI inference happens elsewhere.

Presumably, this is the model AMD is aiming at with Helion as hyperscalers build out CPU capacity on the back of agentic AI. However, the design is flexible, supporting up to 16 MI350P GPUs and 102 Tbps of networking, though at the cost of CPU capacity. This hybrid configuration is targeted at enterprises, says AMD, giving them an all-in-one rack for data management, networking, and AI usage.
AMD says the Helion rack will be available starting in the first half of 2027, likely riding the wave of Zen 6 deployments that are expected to start ramping up later this year.

candidato.resumo: NASA experiments focused on human and plant health and drug-resistant organisms will travel to the International Space Station aboard SpaceX’s 35th Commercial Resupply Services mission for the agency from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, advancing research that benefits life on Earth and future exploration. texto_fonte:
NASA experiments focused on human and plant health and drug-resistant organisms will travel to the International Space Station aboard SpaceX’s 35th Commercial Resupply Services mission for the agency from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, advancing research that benefits life on Earth and future exploration.
This research supports astronaut health during long-duration missions through four investigations from the agency’s Biological and Physical Sciences division, including 3D models of the human brain, a crop disease study, a faster way to assess astronaut health, and an analysis of antibiotic-resistant bacteria aboard the space station.
Tiny brain models, big questions
A new precision health investigation helps address a key question: What happens to the human brain in space?
The experiment sends small, lab-grown models of the human brain to the orbiting laboratory for five weeks. Researchers compare tissue models that traveled to space with identical ones kept on Earth to determine how a short spaceflight affects the human brain at the cellular level.
The effort could deepen our understanding of how the human brain responds to stress and help lay the groundwork for methods that counter risks to brain health that astronauts may face on future missions to the Moon and beyond.
Disease-resistant crops for space
A space crops investigation tests whether crop diseases develop faster and more severely in microgravity.
The experiment compares molecular and structural changes between Earth-grown and space station-grown plants infected with a disease-causing fungus. The findings could guide plant breeding on Earth to produce disease-resistant crops and help minimize yield losses in future space agriculture systems.
Space crops provide nutrition, increase dietary variety, and offer psychological benefits for astronauts during extended missions. They also absorb carbon dioxide, produce oxygen, and recycle water, which will become increasingly important as human missions extend farther from Earth.
Analysis helps astronauts thrive
The spacecraft also carries the first test of a compact microplate reader that arrived aboard the space station earlier this year.
The Commercially Enabled Rapid Space Science initiative experiment tests the device’s ability to detect and measure certain biomarkers such as antibodies, antigens, and proteins.
Use of the plate reader would allow scientists to analyze samples aboard the space station and obtain data quickly, rather than wait for the samples to return to Earth for analysis.
Ultimately, the research aims to support the timely detection of infections and other health issues in astronauts while expanding science capabilities in remote exploration locations where resupply will be more difficult.
Tracking antibiotic-resistant bacteria
A precision health investigation returns for its fourth and final planned stay aboard the space station to study how antibiotic-resistant bacteria survive and evolve in microgravity.
As part of the investigation, astronauts repeatedly sample surfaces throughout the space station to monitor for drug-resistant organisms.
The work could help develop ways to protect astronauts against bacterial infections during long-duration missions. On Earth, the findings could provide insight into how superbugs develop from the overuse of antibiotics.
To learn more about NASA’s biological and physical research in space, visit: https://science.nasa.gov/biological-physical/

Insider Brief
- Penn-led researchers used a photonic chip to transfer a winding pattern from one photon to a shared two-photon state, preserving the pattern under noise even after entanglement disappeared.
- The winding pattern remained stable as the quantum state deteriorated, supported by other quantum correlations, but broke down under sufficiently strong noise.
- The findings could one day be used in the development of more resilient quantum networks.
University of Pennsylvania researchers have used a photonic chip to transfer a winding pattern in quantum light that survived noise even after entanglement disappeared, which they say could help develop quantum networks.
Currently, scientists and engineers are exploring ways to create a quantum network that could, for example, connect two quantum computers in separate buildings so they can work together on a calculation. The team suggests this experiment could be an initial step on the path toward more resilient links between those extremely sensitive quantum systems.
The study, published in Nature Physics, demonstrates a way to create and manipulate quantum skyrmions, which are structured patterns in light whose overall winding can remain stable even as their underlying quantum state deteriorates. To picture this, think how a rope can bend and stretch without losing its knot. In this case, these light patterns can retain their overall winding even as noise degrades their quantum state.
The researchers transferred that structure from a single photon to correlations shared between two photons.
According to the study, the silicon nitride chip combined components that generated photon pairs, routed the photons and shaped the light into skyrmions.
Connecting quantum computers and other quantum devices is challenging because noise — which can include anything from heat to cosmic rays — can weaken the delicate relationships that carry quantum information, making it difficult to move that information reliably between systems.
However, this experiment has a tighter scope than demonstrating a working, noise-resistant quantum network. The scientists preserved a particular measurable property of the light, rather than showing that an entire quantum state could be transmitted intact after entanglement was lost. They point out that the experiment does not establish a practical advantage for quantum state transfer.
A Pattern That Holds Its Shape
A photon, which is a particle of light, has a quantum state that can include polarization — the orientation and motion of light’s electric field — and spatial properties associated with how the light’s wavefront is arranged.
In these skyrmions, the orientation of light’s electric field changes from place to place, forming a winding pattern. That pattern is described by a skyrmion number, which counts how many times the polarization arrangement covers the full set of possible polarization states.
The researchers write that the underlying idea comes from topology, the study of properties that remain unchanged when a structure is smoothly deformed. Individual parts of a pattern can move or change without altering its overall winding.
For quantum technology, this is important because a disturbance might degrade many details of a light-based quantum state while leaving its topological number recognizable.
According to the study, earlier research had produced single-photon skyrmions on chips and skyrmions shared between entangled photons using larger optical arrangements. The new work brings preparation and manipulation into an integrated platform and demonstrates a transfer between the two forms.
Entanglement is a quantum relationship where the particles are linked so that measuring one offers information about the other, even when they are far apart. Quantum networks rely on these links, but noise and other disturbances can disrupt them.
The Penn-led team found that the above mentioned skyrmion number could remain preserved over a finite range of noise after a standard measure of entanglement fell to zero. Other quantum correlations also persisted, helping sustain the winding structure, according to the researchers’ analysis.
How the Chip Transferred the Structure
The researchers used short laser pulses to generate photon pairs in two spiral channels on the chip. The photons were separated by wavelength and routed through an array of optical components controlled by tiny electrical heaters.
One photon passed through ring-shaped structures that created the skyrmion pattern. These structures linked its polarization with orbital angular momentum, a property associated with a twisting light wavefront.
The second photon was directed through a component that converted its on-chip paths into different polarizations.
By measuring two properties of the first photon together, the researchers transferred its winding pattern into a pattern shared between the two photons. The structure was then carried by the relationship between the photons, rather than by one photon alone.
The researchers reconstructed the quantum states through repeated measurements, a process called quantum state tomography. This allowed them to assess both how closely the resulting states matched their intended form and whether the winding number survived.
For the principal demonstration, the intended skyrmion number was 2. Measurements of the transferred states yielded values close to 1.98. The four measurement outcomes produced states with fidelities ranging from 87% to 89%, according to the study.
Fidelity measures how closely the quantum state produced in the experiment matches the intended state. When the team added noise, that match worsened, but the light’s overall winding pattern remained largely unchanged.
Testing the Limits of Resilience
To test that stability, the researchers deliberately introduced background noise and adjustable white-light noise. The added noise affected the different measurement settings almost equally, approximating a type of disturbance known as depolarization.
As the noise increased, the measured states became less pure and their fidelity declined. Their skyrmion number, however, remained near its original value even after entanglement vanished.
The team assessed the remaining quantum correlations using a measure called quantum discord. Unlike entanglement, discord can remain present in some noisy states that are no longer entangled.
According to the researchers, its persistence indicates that the surviving topology was associated with quantum correlations beyond entanglement. That does not mean any remaining quantum correlation is sufficient to protect the pattern indefinitely. The study reports that topology can break down before discord reaches zero.
Under sufficiently strong background noise, the skyrmion number collapsed toward zero. The protection therefore had a limit.
The team also examined two more targeted types of error. One changed the relative phase between parts of the quantum state, affecting how they combine. The other combined a phase change with a swap between the encoded alternatives.
For these tests, the researchers used controlled chip operations and numerical mixtures of measured photon counts to represent different error strengths. The winding number again remained stable as fidelity declined, until the disturbance approached the tested critical threshold.
Numerical simulations reproduced the main behavior observed in the experiments. Some measured results deteriorated earlier than an idealized noise model predicted, which the researchers attributed to small additional disturbances that did not affect every measurement setting equally.
Toward Quantum Interconnects
The study suggests that topology could offer an additional property to track or exploit when designing connections between quantum systems. It also provides a chip-based platform for investigating how that property behaves under noise.
Existing approaches such as quantum error correction and entanglement purification aim to protect or restore quantum information, but can require substantial resources and precise control, the researchers write.
The new experiment, however, does not conclusively establish that skyrmions can replace those methods. Its immediate contribution is a demonstration that a quantum light pattern can be prepared, manipulated and transferred while retaining its winding number under conditions that destroy entanglement.
Future work would need to determine whether that resilience can support a useful information-processing task. The researchers identify protocols involving noisy quantum states as a direction for further investigation, alongside efforts to encode and read out topological properties of light.
For quantum networking, the open question is whether preserving this limited but durable feature can help devices communicate more reliably. The chip gives researchers a way to test that possibility.
The team included Haoqi Zhao, Yichi Zhang, Shuang Wu, Yaoyang Ji and Liang Feng of the University of Pennsylvania; Isaac Nape and Andrew Forbes of the University of the Witwatersrand in South Africa; and Chenjie Zhang and Yijie Shen of Nanyang Technological University in Singapore.

If you buy an external SSD or a USB stick today that’s being offered at a bargain price with astronomical storage capacities, you should be rather skeptical. The reason: The market is currently being flooded with sophisticated counterfeit storage devices.
Manipulated controller firmware can trick the operating system into believing the device has more capacity than physically exists. Here’s an example: Imagine you’ve bought a supposed 4TB SSD on a well-known online platform and your Windows Explorer also displays this capacity.
In reality, however, the drive contains only a comparatively tiny 64GB chip. The insidious thing about this manipulation is that the controller has been programmed to appear to acknowledge write operations successfully, even when the physical storage has long since been exhausted.
Samsung
As soon as the actual capacity is exceeded, the drive either starts overwriting the oldest data at the beginning of the storage or simply dumps new data packets into a digital black hole, while the file system continues to report an intact structure.
The rude awakening usually only sets in weeks later, when you try to open your supposedly backed-up holiday photos or documents. Instead of the content, you’ll only get error messages or find corrupted file fragments. We must make this absolutely clear: The operating system is not a reliable indicator of a drive’s integrity.
It merely retrieves the information provided by the controller. And in this case, the controller has been tampered with. To expose these deceptions, you need tools that scrutinize every single bit. You should therefore check every new drive immediately upon receipt using the Validrive tool: Launch the program with administrator rights and select ‘Check USB Drive.’
Foundry
Now insert the storage device and allow the program to recognize it. Click on ‘Validate THIS drive’ to start the check. The tool carries out a quick, targeted check by writing to random sectors across the entire declared range and reading them back immediately.
As Validrive measures and analyzes access times during this process, it is able to determine very quickly whether there is actually a physical cell behind a logical address, or whether the controller is simply suppressing an error message.

If you’ve ever wondered how Claude and similar AI agents can answer complex questions in seconds and where they get the information, you’re not alone.
Gurmeet Saran works to find that answer every day as an engineer at Anthropic in San Francisco, the AI research company behind Claude. The IEEE senior member is developing an infrastructure to understand the mechanics behind the chatbot’s behavior and to ensure its underlying architecture produces reliable outputs.

“My job is to make sure the data is accurate, structured, and trustworthy, and that private data stays private,” he says. “As I learned earlier in my career, privacy can’t be a layer you bolt on—it has to be part of the architecture from the start.” If you can’t trust the logic, he adds, you can’t make reliable claims about the behavior, and that has real safety implications.
Safety is a priority for Anthropic, he says. According to Claude’s mission statement, the company wants the AI agent to be “genuinely helpful to the people it works with or on behalf of, as well as to society, while avoiding actions that are unsafe, unethical, or deceptive.” Crucial to the mission is ensuring that researchers can observe and understand how AI models behave, a challenge that is especially acute for large language models, Saran says.
“We have decent tools to monitor databases and web services,” he says, “but for LLMs, we’re still figuring it out.”
Saran’s interest in computing systems dates back to his childhood in Kolkata, where he logged as much time as he could in the school computer lab.
“I remember the first time I used one of the computers,” he says. “What struck me was that you could write instructions, and the machine would follow them exactly. No ambiguity.
“That felt magical to me.”
After graduating from high school in 1999, he stayed in India to pursue advanced degrees. He earned a bachelor’s degree in electronics and telecommunication engineering in 2004 at the University of Kalyani. In 2010, he earned a master’s degree in software engineering from the Birla Institute of Technology and Science in Pilani.
While a graduate student, he began his career in 2007 at Yahoo as a technical lead of the data team in Bengaluru, India. While there, he encountered the project that shaped his career trajectory: working on web analytics and business intelligence reporting solutions.
“We kept running into a frustrating problem,” he recalls. “Different teams would calculate the same website metric—something like daily active site users—using slightly different logic, and end up with conflicting answers. It sounds like a small issue, but when leadership is making decisions about resource allocation and product development using that data, not knowing which number is correct becomes a problem.”
The team built a central data repository with defined metrics, essentially serving as a single source of truth. Saran created a model that defined what “daily active site users” means, breaking down which events counted, how to handle edge cases (or when standard code fails), and more.
With the new model, data teams across the company could rely on a standard method to determine the number of daily active users for the projects and sites they were responsible for and obtain comparable results using the same logic.
From there, Saran and his team built Yahoo! Digits, an internal web analytics tool used for all the company’s products.
Saran left Yahoo in 2010 to join Intuit as a staff engineer in Mountain View, Calif. He helped build the analytics infrastructure that unified data across the company’s products, including TurboTax and QuickBooks accounting software. During his tenure, Intuit developed a feature that detected fraudulent tax filings in real time. It required Saran and other engineers to build a system to protect taxpayer data while adhering to strict U.S. Internal Revenue Service policies.
“IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. That kind of connection matters as AI development spreads beyond a handful of organizations.”
“This taught me that privacy and governance can’t be layers you bolt onto software after the fact,” he says. “They have to be part of the architecture from the start.”
Saran joined Meta (known as Facebook at the time) in 2016 as a lead software engineer in Menlo Park, Calif. The company was facing controversy over its video metrics: Meta publicly acknowledged an error that caused it to overstate the number of views for posted videos.
“This wasn’t a coding bug; it was an architectural problem,” Saran says. He built a system that worked similarly to what he had developed at Intuit, whereby one single truth was defined to govern all video view metrics across the site.
That system, Metric360, eventually became part of the site’s architecture. By the time he left Meta in 2021, he says, Metric360 was being used across the company to calculate video metrics.
He left the company to become a principal software engineer at Wealthfront, a financial services company in Palo Alto, Calif. He helped build the company’s data infrastructure.
Building trustworthy AI systems at Anthropic
Saran joined Anthropic in 2025 as a member of the technical staff.
To describe the implications of his work, he uses a medical analogy: “Imagine a doctor is monitoring a patient’s vital signs and making treatment decisions based on those numbers. What if one or a few of the medical devices used were slightly miscalibrated? Even if most readings are fine, it’s a serious problem because the difficult decisions happen in the margins.
“It’s the same with AI systems. My job is essentially to make sure the instruments are giving accurate readings—that the data means what it says it means.”
His job comes with high stakes and complex problems to solve.
“AI agents are especially tricky to observe,” he says. “When a system is taking sequences of actions [generating conversational responses with different users], you need a way to capture what it did, what information it was working from, and whether outcomes matched what the end user expected. And you have to do all of that without exposing anyone’s private information—the systems are designed to recognize sensitive data and keep it protected as it flows through. It’s a much more demanding observability problem than anything I’ve worked on before.”
Solving for system reliability while AI is still in its early days of adoption is both Saran’s passion and the problem that keeps him up at night, he says.
“I think making AI systems genuinely auditable and transparent is one of the more important engineering problems of the next decade,” he says, “and it doesn’t get talked about as much as model capabilities do.”
IEEE can play a role in shaping AI development
Saran joined IEEE in March 2025.
“After more than 20 years of building data infrastructure across organizations like Yahoo, Intuit, Meta, and Wealthfront,” he says, “I wanted to contribute back to the technical community through peer review, publishing, and engaging with the broader engineering research ecosystem.”
He says he believes IEEE can play an essential role in shaping the future of AI through its standards work.
“We have standards for everything, from building codes to software testing,” he says. “AI infrastructure needs something similar, and IEEE has the credibility and the reach to do that.”
Another problem that IEEE can solve for, he says, is access: “IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. That kind of connection matters, especially as AI development spreads beyond a handful of organizations in a few cities.”

candidato.titulo: O que significa o ícone de escudo na bateria do Samsung Galaxy?
candidato.resumo: O ícone de escudo ao lado da bateria em um celular Samsung Galaxy pode parecer um alerta de segurança, mas sua função está relacionada à preservação da bateria. O símbolo indica que a “ Proteção da bateria” está ativa no aparelho. Os celulares atuais usam baterias de íons de lítio, que sofrem desgaste natural ao longo do tempo. Manter o componente em 100% de carga por períodos prolongados pode acelerar esse processo, especialmente quando o aparelho permanece conectado à tomada por muitas horas. Para reduzir o desgaste, a Samsung oferece recursos que controlam o carregamento de acordo com o modo escolhido. As opções disponíveis podem variar conforme o modelo do Galaxy e a versão da One UI, inclusive em alguns modelos Galaxy, os recursos de “Proteção da bateria” podem vir ativados por padrão de fábrica. Como funciona a proteção da bateria nos celulares Galaxy? Quando a “Proteção da bateria” está ativada, o sistema modifica o carregamento para reduzir o tempo em que a bateria permanece em níveis elevados.
